THE INVESTMENT

Why this deserves your time.

Linux is common in robotics development, and many scientific tools are comfortable at the command line. You already have a Windows-oriented workflow; Ubuntu through WSL can provide a Linux practice environment. Basic shell fluency reduces setup friction when you later meet ROS 2, build systems, remote computers, and batches of simulations.

You do not need to become a system administrator. The valuable foundation is understanding paths, processes, permissions, inputs, outputs, and exit codes. Small reliable scripts can save hours and make your results easier to reproduce.

Connect it to your existing tools

Bash ties together Python scripts, C/C++ builds, ROS 2 environments, logs, and repeated simulator runs. It is supporting infrastructure for the other languages rather than an equally large daily study commitment.

FROM SYNTAX TO SYSTEMS

Problems this helps you solve.

01

Batch experiments

Run the same Python analysis for several data files, saving output under clear names. Record the command and configuration used for each run.

02

Robot operations

Inspect logs and running processes on a Linux computer. Later, use SSH to reach a machine you control and understand which machine a command will affect.

03

Build and test

Run a compiler, a test suite, or a ROS build command consistently. A failed command should be visible before downstream steps continue.

04

Data preparation

Select relevant log lines and count events. Move to Python when a task becomes complex data processing rather than a small pipeline.

THE HONEST LEARNING CURVE

What is hard—and why.

You can get useful results quickly. Reliable scripting is harder because the shell expands variables, patterns, and command substitutions before running programs. Quoting, whitespace, exit codes, pipes, and portability create subtle bugs.

Linux is not a programming language

Linux is an operating-system family; Ubuntu is a distribution. Bash is one shell and scripting language. Git Bash, WSL, and a robot’s Linux computer are different environments.

PowerShell is a different shell

Your Windows terminal may open PowerShell. Bash examples should run in Bash; changing the tab title does not change syntax or the active machine.

Keep scripts small and inspectable

Quote variables, check failures, test with filenames containing spaces, and use ShellCheck. shellcheck does not prove a script is correct.

A trap to avoid

Do not copy commands you cannot explain, especially destructive ones. Start in a disposable practice folder and keep the first scripts read-only.

LEARN IN LAYERS

A sequence with a visible result.

  1. 01 · Orient yourself

    pwd, ls, cd, paths, help, tab completion, and running a program.

    YOUR PROOFFind a project folder, explain the current directory, and run a known script.

  2. 02 · Work with streams

    Standard input/output/error, pipes, grep, head, and exit status.

    YOUR PROOFFilter a sample log and explain each step of the pipeline.

  3. 03 · Repeat a workflow

    Variables, quoting, loops, conditions, and explicit failure handling.

    YOUR PROOFProcess three sample files including one with spaces in its name.

  4. 04 · Support a robot project

    Environment setup, SSH concepts, build commands, logs, reproducibility.

    YOUR PROOFWrite a README that lets you rerun an experiment from a clean terminal.

Advance by understanding, not a promised number of weeks. Rebuild a small example unaided, explain an error, and check a result before adding the next layer.

A SMALL WORKING IDEA

See the reason behind the code.

TRY THE IDEA

Make a log answer one question.

Change the control and predict the result before looking.

A browser illustration of fixed sample data, not a terminal. These commands select and count text; they do not change the source log.

Bash / Linux / EXAMPLE TO STUDY
# Run this in Bash, inside your practice folder.
for file in "run 1.csv" "run 2.csv"; do
    if ! python analyze.py "$file"; then
        printf "Analysis failed: %s\n" "$file" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
done

Illustration runs in JavaScript in your browser. The Bash / Linux example is separate code to study and run in the appropriate environment.

CURATED, NOT COLLECTED

One main path. A few useful companions.

Start Software Carpentry’s Unix Shell lesson or The Linux Command Line. Use the Bash manual and ShellCheck as references; take a broader Linux course only if you need the structure.

THE NEXT SMALL WIN

In a practice folder, run pwd and ls, then display the first five lines of a sample log with head. Explain what each command does before using a pipeline.

A useful session ends with evidence

  1. Predict. What should happen, and why?
  2. Write. Spend most of the time in code.
  3. Check. Try a simple value and an awkward one.
  4. Explain. Describe the result in your own words.

Use AI for hints, explanations, and review. Attempt the task first, follow course rules, and finish by solving a small variant unaided.

EVIDENCE OF PROGRESS

Could you do it without a walkthrough?

A PROJECT WORTH KEEPING

Make a repeatable telemetry-review script. Run a Python analyzer for three sample CSV files, keep the reports separate, and stop with a readable message if an input file is missing.

Save the code, sample input, a short README, assumptions and units, a test case, and a result you can explain. That is stronger evidence than a completed playlist.
